column1: # ---------- retake batch: acr-appservice (retake1) ----------
Two ways to address an ACR artifact when pulling — which one can silently change, and which is reproducible?
column2: Addressing by tag (repo:v1.2.0) is mutable — a later push to the same tag moves it to new bytes. Addressing by digest (repo@sha256:<hash>, the manifest's own hash) is immutable, so pulling by digest guarantees every node gets the exact same image — the production-reproducibility answer.

column1: Exam scenario: a reviewer claims every advanced ACR capability requires the Premium tier. Which pair is actually available on Basic and Standard too?
column2: Availability-zone redundancy and repository-scoped tokens/scope maps are supported on all three tiers — only the token/scope-map quantity limit scales up (100 / 500 / 50,000 on Basic/Standard/Premium). True Premium-only features are geo-replication, private link/private endpoints, content trust, customer-managed keys, dedicated data endpoints, and the registry-level retention policy for untagged manifests. A third group — anonymous pull access and artifact cache rules — needs Standard or above: not on Basic, but also not Premium-exclusive.

column1: How do you stop a production ACR image tag from being deleted or overwritten?
column2: Lock it: az acr repository update --name <registry> --image <repo:tag> --write-enabled false. A locked tag can't be deleted or overwritten (even by an admin) and survives acr purge/retention cleanup; reverse it with --write-enabled true before retiring the tag.

column1: How do you clean up orphaned untagged ACR images, and what's the Premium-only shortcut?
column2: Run acr purge inside the registry: az acr run --registry <reg> --cmd "acr purge --filter 'repo:.*' --untagged --ago 30d" /dev/null, typically scheduled as a cron ACR Task for recurring cleanup. Premium tier adds a simpler registry-wide retention policy for untagged manifests that needs no scheduled task at all.

column1: How do you copy an image into Azure Container Registry from Docker Hub or another registry without a local Docker install?
column2: az acr import --name <registry> --source docker.io/library/nginx:latest --image nginx:latest — works from public registries, another ACR, or a private non-Azure registry, and copies multi-architecture manifests (max 50 per image). Requires the Container Registry Data Importer and Data Reader role; available on every SKU tier.

column1: ACR's classic data-plane roles — what does each of AcrPull, AcrPush, and AcrDelete actually grant?
column2: AcrPull: read-only pull of images/artifacts/tags. AcrPush: push + pull + manage tags, but no delete. AcrDelete: delete artifacts and tags across the registry, but does not grant permission to delete the registry resource itself — that needs a control-plane role like Contributor.

column1: ACR's admin user account — enabled by default? How many passwords does it have?
column2: Disabled by default on every new registry; enable with az acr update --name <registry> --admin-enabled true. It has two independent passwords so you can regenerate one while the other keeps authenticating — but all callers share one identity, so Microsoft recommends individual Entra/managed-identity auth instead for anything beyond quick testing.

column1: You're scripting in Azure Cloud Shell, which has the Docker CLI but no running Docker daemon. How do you still get an ACR login token?
column2: az acr login --name <registry> --expose-token returns a raw access token instead of driving docker login through the daemon — pipe it into docker login <registry>.azurecr.io --username 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000 --password-stdin. Normal az acr login needs the Docker daemon and its Entra token expires after 3 hours either way.

column1: az acr build vs az acr run — what's the key difference?
column2: az acr build sends a source context (Dockerfile + files) to ACR and builds a new image, then pushes it. az acr run instead executes an existing image already in the registry (e.g. az acr run -r <reg> --cmd "api:v1 pytest" /dev/null) — no build step, just a cloud-hosted smoke test or health check against what's already there.

column1: ACR Tasks quick build — what source-context locations does az acr build accept?
column2: A local directory (uploaded and compressed by the CLI), a Git repository URL (public or private GitHub/Azure DevOps, built without a local clone), or a remote tarball URL. The trailing . in az acr build -r reg -t img:tag . just means "local directory is the context".

column1: Exam scenario: an ACR base-image-update trigger is configured, but an application image built FROM a privately-hosted base image in a different, unrelated registry never rebuilds automatically. Why?
column2: Base-image triggers only auto-detect updates when the base image lives in the same ACR registry as the dependent image, or in a public registry (Docker Hub, MCR, etc.). A private base image hosted in a different private registry isn't watched, so the dependent image is never rebuilt automatically — move the base image into the same registry or add a scheduled/commit trigger instead.

column1: How do you grant an ACR Task its own identity to pull/push cross-registry or read a Key Vault secret, without embedding credentials in the task?
column2: az acr task create ... --assign-identity [<user-identity-resourceID>] (omit the value for system-assigned). Grant the identity a role on the target resource — use AcrPull on a classic (non-ABAC) registry, or Container Registry Repository Reader on an ABAC-enabled registry — then the running task authenticates as that identity automatically.

column1: Deploying a container to App Service from ACR — what are the two supported pull-authentication choices, and which does Microsoft recommend?
column2: Managed identity (system- or user-assigned, granted the AcrPull role on the registry) is the recommended production choice — no stored secret, no rotation burden. Admin credentials (registry admin user + password as app settings) is simpler for quick testing but requires az acr update --admin-enabled true and shares one account across every caller.

column1: Which App Service setting switches a container's ACR image pull from admin credentials to managed identity?
column2: az webapp config set --generic-configurations '{"acrUseManagedIdentityCreds": true}'. For a user-assigned identity, also set its client ID with acrUserManagedIdentityID — otherwise App Service assumes the web app's system-assigned identity.

column1: Exam scenario: a document-processing container writes output to disk, but every file disappears after the app restarts. What's the fix, and what's the gotcha for Windows containers?
column2: Set WEBSITES_ENABLE_APP_SERVICE_STORAGE=true so /home persists across restarts and is shared by every scaled-out instance — it's disabled by default on Linux custom containers. Gotcha: Windows containers have it enabled by default for C:\home, the opposite default, so a lift-and-shift from Windows to Linux silently loses persistence unless you flip the setting.

column1: What does App Service's always-on setting do, and what tier does it require?
column2: Keeps the app loaded by sending periodic pings, eliminating the cold start that follows roughly 20 minutes of idle time — important for large images or slow-initializing models. Requires the Basic pricing tier or higher (not available on Free/Shared).

column1: App Service container health checks — how often does the platform probe, and what happens after repeated failures?
column2: App Service pings the configured health-check path about once a minute; after 10 consecutive failures on an instance, that instance is pulled out of the load-balancer rotation (and can be replaced if it stays unhealthy). Your endpoint should return HTTP 200 only when real dependencies (DB, storage) are actually reachable.

column1: A Key Vault reference is set as an App Service app setting (@Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=...)). What does App Service need to resolve it, and how fast does a secret rotation show up?
column2: The web app needs a managed identity that's been granted read access to the vault's secrets. An unversioned reference auto-refreshes within about 24 hours of a secret rotation, or immediately on any config change that forces an app restart — don't assume a rotated secret is live instantly without a restart.

column1: What are App Service slot settings, and when do you use --slot-settings instead of a normal app setting?
column2: Settings marked with --slot-settings (e.g. an ENVIRONMENT or API-endpoint value) stay attached to the slot, not the code, during a slot swap — so staging keeps pointing at staging resources even after the swap promotes the container image to production. Normal app settings swap WITH the code by default.

column1: App Service connection strings get a type prefix on their environment-variable name — name the prefixes for SQL Server, Azure SQL, MySQL, and PostgreSQL.
column2: SQLCONNSTR_, SQLAZURECONNSTR_, MYSQLCONNSTR_, and POSTGRESQLCONNSTR_ (custom type uses CUSTOMCONNSTR_). This prefixing mainly benefits .NET's ConfigurationManager auto-binding — non-.NET apps on Linux containers are usually simpler to configure with a plain app setting instead of a typed connection string.

column1: You update an ACR image under the SAME tag the running App Service app already uses. Does the app pick up the new bytes automatically?
column2: No — App Service only re-pulls on restart/scale-out, so a same-tag repush is invisible until something restarts the app. Enable az webapp deployment container config --enable-cd true to get a webhook URL, wire it to the registry's push event, and every push then triggers an automatic pull + restart.

column1: A custom container app returns connection errors or 404s right after deployment. What's the triage order, and the two classic root causes?
column2: First az webapp log tail for live stdout/stderr, then the Kudu/SCM site's /Env page to confirm which environment variables actually reached the container. The two classic root causes: WEBSITES_PORT doesn't match the port the app listens on, or the app bound to localhost instead of 0.0.0.0 so the platform's traffic never reaches it.

column1: Container logs on App Service repeatedly show a 404 for GET /robots933456.txt. Is this a bug?
column2: No — it's App Service's own internal readiness probe hitting a deliberately-nonexistent path to confirm the container can serve HTTP requests at all. A 404 response is the healthy result; it's safe to ignore in your logs and doesn't indicate a routing problem.

column1: What is the CURRENT status of classic Docker Compose ("multi-container") support on Azure App Service?
column2: Still functional but in preview (4,000-character compose-file limit; no Auth/Authorization, no managed identity, no CORS, no VNet integration) and officially retiring on 2027-03-31. Microsoft's documented migration path for both new and existing multi-container apps is the sidecar feature, not Docker Compose.

column1: App Service sidecars: how many containers can an app have, how are roles assigned, and how do they talk to each other?
column2: One main container (isMain: true) plus up to nine sidecars (isMain: false); only the main container receives external HTTP traffic, and it must listen on port 80 or 8080 (classic WEBSITES_PORT doesn't apply to this model). All containers share one network namespace, so they call each other at localhost:<port> — never by container name — and every listening process needs a unique port.

column1: How do main and sidecar containers on App Service exchange files without extra configuration?
column2: They automatically share the default /home volume (e.g. /home/models/manifest.json) — no volumeMounts entry needed — unless WEBSITES_ENABLE_APP_SERVICE_STORAGE is set to false. Write to a temp filename and rename it into place so a reader never sees a partially-written file; treat anything needing real durability as a job for Azure Storage instead.

column1: A sidecar-enabled App Service app pulls its images from an Azure Container Registry. Which role does the managed identity need — and why might the answer differ per registry?
column2: AcrPull when the registry uses the classic RBAC Registry Permissions mode; Container Registry Repository Reader when the registry uses RBAC Registry + ABAC Repository Permissions mode (so the grant can optionally be scoped to one repository). Check the registry's permission mode under its Properties before assuming AcrPull is always correct.

column1: What are Microsoft's prebuilt App Service sidecar extensions, and why are they relevant to AI apps specifically?
column2: Officially supported prebuilt sidecars include small local AI models (Phi-3 / Phi-4) for on-box inference and a local Redis cache — drop-in containers you configure instead of hand-rolling. They exist precisely for the "one compact model or cache per app instance, same lifecycle as the API" pattern the sidecar model targets.

column1: # ---------- retake batch: aca-aks (retake1) ----------
Container Apps ingress: targetPort vs exposedPort — what's the difference?
column2: targetPort is the port your container listens on for HTTP ingress — the public HTTP endpoint is always published on port 443 regardless of this value. exposedPort only applies to TCP ingress: the actual port number (1-65535, never 80 or 443) that TCP clients connect to.

column1: Exam scenario: a Container App has HTTP ingress enabled, no targetPort set, and the container listens on exactly one port. What does Container Apps do?
column2: It uses automatic port detection: it scans the container's listening ports and, since only one is found, sets it as targetPort automatically. If two or more candidate ports are found it does not guess — you must set targetPort manually. Automatic detection only works for HTTP ingress, never TCP.

column1: Discriminator: Container Apps external vs internal ingress — what exactly differs?
column2: External publishes the app through the environment's own inbound IP, and other apps in the same environment can still reach it. Internal publishes the app's FQDN only inside the same environment — a request to the environment's inbound IP for an internal app returns HTTP 404, even though the app is still reachable by name from inside the environment.

column1: Exam trap: a Container Apps environment is created with --internal-only, and an app in it has ingress set to external ('Accepting traffic from anywhere'). Is it reachable from the public internet?
column2: No. Ingress visibility is relative to the environment, not the internet. An internal environment has no public endpoint at all, so an external app there is published only at the environment's internal load balancer — reachable from the connected virtual network, never from the internet.

column1: Container Apps ingress defaults: allowInsecure and clientCertificateMode?
column2: allowInsecure defaults to false (plain HTTP on port 80 auto-redirects to HTTPS). clientCertificateMode defaults to Ignore (mTLS client cert dropped) — the other values are Accept (forwarded but not required) and Require.

column1: Does changing a Container App's ingress settings (traffic weights, IP restrictions, transport) create a new revision?
column2: No — ingress is an application-scope setting. Changes apply to all revisions immediately and never generate a new revision, unlike revision-scope changes such as the container image or scale rules.

column1: Container Apps stickySessions.affinity values, and what it does?
column2: none (default) or sticky. sticky pins a client to the same replica across requests via a cookie — useful for in-memory session state, at the cost of even load distribution.

column1: Container Apps: which changes create a NEW revision — the image/scale rules/env vars, or secrets/ingress/traffic-split weights?
column2: Revision-scope changes (container image, scale rules, env vars, other template properties) create a new revision. Application-scope changes (secrets, ingress settings, traffic-splitting weights) do not. Trap: many assume editing a secret creates a revision — it does not; existing revisions keep the old value until redeployed or restarted.

column1: Container Apps single revision mode: how is a deploy 'zero-downtime' without the team hand-managing traffic splits?
column2: The new revision is provisioned and must pass its health checks and reach the previous revision's replica count before any traffic shifts to it; only then does the old revision deactivate automatically. You don't configure traffic weights yourself in single mode.

column1: How many inactive Container Apps revisions are retained by default?
column2: 100 inactive revisions by default (the threshold can be adjusted).

column1: Exam scenario (mock01 fix): a Container Apps worker must scale out with a Service Bus queue backlog and scale to zero when the queue is empty. Give the exact scale-rule fields.
column2: A custom KEDA rule with type: azure-servicebus, metadata: {queueName, messageCount}, an auth block with a secretRef pointing at a Container Apps secret holding the connection string, and minReplicas: 0. Trap: an http or tcp/cpu rule cannot see Service Bus queue depth at all — only a custom event-driven scaler can.
column3: ai200::containers aca keda servicebus mock01 retake1

column1: Container Apps scale limits: default minReplicas/maxReplicas, and the hard ceiling?
column2: minReplicas defaults to 0 (range 0-1000); maxReplicas defaults to 10 (range 1-1000). 1000 replicas is the hard ceiling for either value.

column1: Container Apps: what happens when a replica exceeds its CPU limit vs its memory limit?
column2: Exceeding the CPU limit throttles the replica (slower, not killed). Exceeding the memory limit gets the replica terminated and restarted. Default allocation is 0.25 vCPU / 0.5 GiB per container, and memory (GiB) must be at least 2× the vCPU core count.

column1: Container Apps: non-HTTP/TCP (custom event-driven) scale rules require which activeRevisionsMode?
column2: single. Custom KEDA scale rules (Service Bus, Event Hubs, Kafka, Redis, CPU, memory, ...) are only supported when the app is in single revision mode.

column1: Exam scenario: a Container App has only an HTTP scaling rule, but it's really a Service Bus queue worker. The backlog grows to 10,000 messages and replicas stay at 1. Why, and the fix?
column2: The HTTP scaler only counts concurrent HTTP requests to the revision's endpoint — it has no visibility into Service Bus. Add or replace it with a custom KEDA azure-servicebus scale rule so replica count tracks queue depth.
column3: ai200::containers aca keda servicebus scenario retake1

column1: Container Apps managed identity: system-assigned vs user-assigned — key differences?
column2: System-assigned: exactly one per app, same lifecycle as the app (deleted with it). User-assigned: a standalone resource, an app can have several, and it persists independently of any one app — e.g. one identity shared by many apps to pull from the same registry.

column1: Exam scenario: a Container App must pull its image from a private ACR with zero stored credentials.
column2: Grant the app's managed identity the AcrPull role on the registry and reference the registry by identity — no username/password needed. (Same underlying pattern AKS uses via its kubelet identity and --attach-acr.)
column3: ai200::containers aca identity acr scenario retake1

column1: Discriminator: default health probes — raw Kubernetes/AKS vs Container Apps?
column2: Raw Kubernetes/AKS defines no default probes — an undefined probe means Kubernetes assumes the container is always ready and alive. Container Apps does the opposite: if ingress is enabled and you don't define your own, the platform auto-injects default TCP startup/readiness/liveness probes against the ingress target port.

column1: Container Apps default auto-injected probes: two cases where they are NOT added?
column2: They're never added to sidecar containers (only the main app container), and never added on GPU workload profiles (Dedicated or Consumption GPU).

column1: Container Apps default probes: Startup vs Readiness failureThreshold and period?
column2: Startup: period 1s, failureThreshold 240 (≈ 4 minutes to give up). Readiness: period 5s, failureThreshold 48 (≈ 4 minutes). Both default to a plain TCP check on the ingress target port.

column1: Container Apps Jobs: the three trigger types, one line each?
column2: Manual — started on demand via API/CLI. Schedule — a cron expression (e.g. a nightly report). Event — a KEDA-style custom scale rule triggers executions (e.g. messages waiting in a queue).

column1: Exam scenario: a worker must process a single queued message and then stop, not keep running. App or Job?
column2: A Job with trigger type Event and a custom (e.g. azure-servicebus) scale rule. An app is the wrong answer here: apps are long-running and restart automatically on failure instead of stopping after one unit of work.

column1: Container Apps: name the 3 log categories and their KQL tables.
column2: Console logs (stdout/stderr) → ContainerAppConsoleLogs_CL. System logs (platform events: revision provisioning, traffic-weight changes, domain binding) → ContainerAppSystemLogs_CL. HTTP logs (ingress-layer 5xx/latency/WebSocket) → ContainerAppHTTPLogs (no _CL suffix) — opt-in via diagnostic settings, off by default. The _CL suffix marks the first two as custom Log Analytics tables from the environment's built-in workspace link; HTTP logs instead use the newer resource-specific diagnostic-settings schema.

column1: Container Apps system log: what ErrorCode values appear on a failed revision provision?
column2: ErrImagePull, Timeout, and ContainerCrashing — emitted on the 'Error provisioning revision' system log message.

column1: Container Apps dynamic sessions: the two session pool types?
column2: Code interpreter pool — a built-in container for running untrusted/LLM-generated code (e.g. via LangChain or Semantic Kernel). Custom container pool — bring-your-own image for custom runtime dependencies. Both use Hyper-V isolation and pre-warmed pools for sub-second allocation.

column1: AKS Service types — include the one most decks forget.
column2: ClusterIP (default, internal-only), NodePort (node-ip:port, dev/test), LoadBalancer (provisions an Azure LB + public IP), and ExternalName — maps the Service to an external DNS name with no proxying or load-balancing at all, just a CNAME-style alias.

column1: Discriminator: a Kubernetes Ingress object vs a Service on AKS?
column2: A Service gives Layer-4 routing/load-balancing to a set of Pods. An Ingress object defines Layer-7 HTTP(S) host/path routing rules, but does nothing on its own — it needs an Ingress controller running in the cluster to act on those rules, e.g. the AKS application routing add-on. Time-sensitive (re-check near exam day): the upstream Ingress-NGINX project's maintenance ended March 2026, and Microsoft's own support for the add-on's NGINX ingress resources ends November 2026 — both the managed add-on's NGINX option and self-managed OSS ingress-nginx are affected, not just the unmanaged path. Migrate to the add-on's Gateway-API-based implementation or Application Gateway for Containers.

column1: Exam scenario: kubectl get endpoints my-svc returns an empty list, but the Pods are Running. Root cause and fix?
column2: The Service's spec.selector doesn't match the Pods' labels — a Service only gets endpoints for Pods whose labels it selects. Fix the selector or the Pod template labels so they agree. This is a different failure mode from a wrong targetPort, which still produces endpoints but drops the actual traffic.
column3: ai200::containers aks k8s troubleshoot connectivity scenario retake1

column1: On a Kubernetes Service manifest, what's the difference between port and targetPort?
column2: port is the port the Service itself exposes to callers. targetPort is the port on the container that traffic is forwarded to — they can differ (e.g. port: 80 → targetPort: 8080). If targetPort doesn't match what the container actually listens on, the Service still shows endpoints but connections fail or hang.

column1: AKS scaling: pick the right tool for stateless CPU-driven load, non-parallelizable right-sizing, nodes stuck Pending, and event/queue-driven scale-to-zero.
column2: HPA (CPU/memory/RPS across identical replicas) · VPA (can't scale horizontally — right-sizes resource requests instead) · Cluster Autoscaler (adds/removes nodes when Pods are Pending) · KEDA (external event sources, true scale-to-zero). Never tune HPA and VPA on the same metric — they fight each other.

column1: # ---------- retake batch: cosmos (retake1) ----------
What does Cosmos DB's default indexing policy actually set (mode, automatic, paths)?
column2: indexingMode: consistent, automatic: true, and a single included path /* (index everything); the only path excluded by default is the system _etag property — id and _ts are always indexed and never even appear in the policy.

column1: Exam scenario: you must bulk-load 50M documents as fast as possible and won't query the container until the load finishes. Which indexing-mode change helps, and what do you do after?
column2: Set indexingMode: none during the load (no per-write index maintenance; point reads by id still work, but any query degenerates to a full scan); afterward switch back to consistent and monitor the online index transformation progress before relying on queries.

column1: Cosmos DB indexing policy path syntax: what do /? , /[]/ , and /* each mean?
column2: /? terminates a path to a scalar value (string/number); /[]/ addresses every element of an array (not /0, /1); /* is a wildcard matching everything below that node. Every policy must include or exclude the root /*.

column1: Two indexing paths conflict: included /food/ingredients/nutrition/* vs excluded /food/ingredients/*. Which wins, and why?
column2: The more precise (deeper) path always wins regardless of include/exclude — here the included nutrition sub-path stays indexed while the rest of ingredients is excluded; at equal depth, /a/? beats /a/*.

column1: You switch a container's indexing policy to exclude-by-default (excludedPaths: /*). What indexing gotcha catches teams off guard about the partition key?
column2: The partition key is not auto-indexed under exclude-by-default (unless it's also /id) — you must explicitly add it to includedPaths, or every query filtering on it falls back to a full partition scan and costs far more RU.

column1: When is a composite index REQUIRED (not just helpful) in Cosmos DB for NoSQL?
column2: Whenever a query's ORDER BY clause sorts on two or more properties — without a matching composite index the query fails outright, it doesn't just get slower.

column1: A composite index is built as (category ASC, price DESC). Which ORDER BY queries reuse it for free, and which need a brand-new index?
column2: The exact same sequence/directions works, and so does the fully reversed sequence (category DESC, price ASC) for free; any mixed direction change (e.g. category DESC, price DESC) needs a separate composite index.

column1: Designing a composite index for a query with two equality filters and one range filter — what ordering rule do you follow?
column2: Put equality filters first, then at most one range filter last — each composite index supports only a single range property, so a query with two range filters needs two separate composite indexes.

column1: Why must a vector embedding path (e.g. /embedding) be excluded from the regular range index even though it also has a vector index?
column2: Range/composite indexes store every array element individually — indexing a 1,536-float embedding array that way wastes huge storage/write RU for zero query benefit; add the embedding path to excludedPaths (e.g. /embedding/*) and define it only under vectorIndexes instead.

column1: Cosmos DB vector index dimension limits: what's the hard cap for flat vs quantizedFlat/diskANN?
column2: flat caps at 505 dimensions (exact brute-force scan); quantizedFlat and diskANN both allow up to 4,096 dimensions — a 3,072-dim text-embedding-3-large vector can't use a flat index at all.

column1: Gotcha: you just created a Cosmos container with a diskANN vector index and loaded 40 test rows — per-query RU charge is much higher than you'd expect for such a tiny dataset. Why?
column2: Both quantizedFlat and diskANN need at least 1,000 vectors before the index is effective (enough data for real quantization/graph construction). Below that threshold Cosmos DB silently falls back to an exact brute-force scan — accuracy is actually fine (even perfect), but you lose the RU/latency savings of the approximate index until you cross 1,000 vectors. No manual rebuild step needed once you do — unlike pgvector's IVFFlat, which needs an explicit reindex.

column1: You change a Cosmos DB vector policy's distance function from cosine to euclidean after the container already has data in it. What happens?
column2: Nothing — until you recreate the container. The vector embedding policy and its vector index are immutable after creation; changing path, dimensions, distance function, or index type requires a new container and a data migration.

column1: Which two numeric knobs tune the accuracy/RU trade-off for Cosmos DB diskANN/quantizedFlat indexes, and what are their maximums?
column2: quantizationByteSize (both types, max 512 bytes) controls compression precision; indexingSearchListSize (diskANN only, max 500) controls how many candidates the build scans — raising either improves accuracy at the cost of RU/latency or build time.

column1: How does the Cosmos DB change feed processor scale out across multiple compute instances?
column2: It divides the container's partition key ranges among the available instances; each range's read progress is tracked independently via its own lease document in the lease container, so adding or removing instances just re-balances which ranges each one owns.

column1: What delivery guarantee does the Cosmos DB change feed processor make, and what does that imply for your handler code?
column2: At-least-once delivery — a restart or failover can re-deliver a change already processed, so the delegate/handler must be idempotent (e.g. upsert-by-id) rather than assuming exactly-once semantics.

column1: Which SDKs ship an actual change feed PROCESSOR class (not just the pull model)?
column2: Only .NET and Java — Python and Node.js have no change feed processor library at all; they must use the pull model (query_items_change_feed() in Python) or rely on the Azure Functions Cosmos DB trigger.

column1: What are Cosmos DB's two change feed modes, and what must be enabled before you can use the newer one?
column2: Latest version mode (default, zero config, inserts/updates only) and All versions and deletes mode (GA, captures creates/updates/deletes including intermediate changes) — the latter requires continuous backup (point-in-time restore) enabled on the account first.

column1: Can an Azure Functions Cosmos DB trigger read the All-versions-and-deletes change feed mode?
column2: Only on .NET isolated worker (set the trigger attribute's ChangeFeedMode property to CosmosDBChangeFeedMode.AllVersionsAndDeletes) — Java, Python, and Node.js Functions triggers can't consume that mode and must fall back to the pull model.

column1: In All-versions-and-deletes mode, which connection mode does Cosmos DB always use for requests, regardless of your client configuration?
column2: Gateway mode — this feed mode ignores your app's configured Direct/Gateway setting and always routes over Gateway.

column1: Exam scenario: Mock01 Q22 revisited — a tenant hard-deletes a document and compliance needs proof of exactly what was deleted and when, not just that it's gone. What's the verified, current fix?
column2: Enable continuous backups, then turn on the (now-GA) All versions and deletes change feed mode — it emits an explicit delete record (metadata.operationType: delete, plus timeToLiveExpired). The default Latest version mode still never shows deletes (model those as a soft-delete flag + TTL instead); Python/Node and non-.NET-isolated-worker Functions triggers still can't consume the new mode — only the pull model works there.

column1: Beyond Strong, which OTHER Cosmos DB consistency level also costs 2x read RU (reads from two replicas)?
column2: Bounded Staleness — like Strong, it reads from a minority quorum of two replicas. Session, Consistent Prefix, and Eventual all read from a single replica at 1x RU.

column1: Exam scenario: a Cosmos DB account has multiple WRITE regions (multi-master). Which consistency level is completely off the table, and why?
column2: Strong — a multi-write-region account can't guarantee a zero RPO/RTO failover, and ironically Strong wouldn't even improve write latency there since writes still replicate to every region first. Session, Consistent Prefix, Eventual, and even Bounded Staleness remain usable.

column1: Bounded Staleness lag is defined by K versions or T seconds, whichever comes first. How do the MINIMUM K/T values differ for a single-region vs a multi-region-write account?
column2: Single-region minimum: 10 write operations or 5 seconds. Multi-region (including multi-write-region) minimum jumps to 100,000 write operations or 300 seconds — Bounded Staleness is allowed there but far looser at scale.

column1: In the Python SDK, how do you capture a session token after a write and use it to guarantee read-your-writes on the next query?
column2: Read x-ms-session-token from the write's response headers (e.g. via a response_hook), then pass it back as session_token= on query_items() — session tokens are partition-bound and must be passed explicitly across separate client instances/services.

column1: A custom Cosmos DB RBAC role grants only the executeQuery data action. A service using this role calls container.query_items() and gets an authorization error. What's missing?
column2: The readChangeFeed data action — the SDK's query path requires both executeQuery and readChangeFeed to succeed, even for an ordinary query that never touches the change feed.

column1: Name the two Cosmos DB built-in data-plane RBAC roles and what each grants.
column2: Cosmos DB Built-in Data Reader — readMetadata, point reads, queries, and change feed reads. Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor — the Reader actions plus full container and item write/delete access. Both are distinct from regular Azure RBAC (control-plane) roles.

column1: Python SDK: how do you create a container with BOTH a custom indexing policy and a vector embedding policy in one call?
column2: database.create_container_if_not_exists(id=..., partition_key=..., indexing_policy={...}, vector_embedding_policy={...}) — both policy dicts are accepted directly as keyword arguments on container creation.

column1: Which response header reveals index USE (utilized vs. recommended paths), and how is it different from the RU-charge header?
column2: x-ms-cosmos-index-utilization — only populated when the query sets populate_index_metrics=True (Python SDK >= 4.6.0); the RU cost itself is always in the separate x-ms-request-charge header on every request.

column1: Cosmos DB's VectorDistance() function has two optional parameters beyond the embedding path and query vector — what do they do?
column2: A boolean third argument forces an exact brute-force search (bypassing the vector index) when set true; an optional JSON object argument can override distanceFunction/dataType for that single query instead of using the container's configured policy.

column1: Cosmos DB vector search score ranges: how do you tell cosine similarity and euclidean distance apart at a glance?
column2: cosine (and dotproduct on normalized vectors) returns -1 to +1, higher = more similar; euclidean returns 0 to +infinity, where 0 = identical and larger = more different — don't ORDER BY DESC on a euclidean score expecting the best matches first.

column1: # ---------- retake batch: pgvector (retake1) ----------
The PostgreSQL community calls it pgvector - what name must you use for CREATE EXTENSION and the azure.extensions allow-list?
column2: Just vector - the binary/extension name is vector, not pgvector; allow-list it first with az postgres flexible-server parameter set --name azure.extensions --value vector, then run CREATE EXTENSION vector;.

column1: Which Azure Database for PostgreSQL compute tier cannot use the built-in PgBouncer, and what port does PgBouncer listen on once enabled?
column2: Burstable cannot enable built-in PgBouncer - only General Purpose and Memory Optimized tiers support it. Once enabled, connect on port 6432 instead of the direct Postgres port 5432.
column3: ai200::data pgvector postgres pgbouncer connection retake1

column1: PgBouncer's three pooling modes, and which one does Azure recommend for typical vector-search workloads?
column2: Session (connection held for the whole session - no LISTEN/NOTIFY or multi-statement limits), transaction (connection returned to the pool after each commit/rollback - the default, and recommended for vector search), and statement (connection per statement - breaks multi-statement transactions).
column3: ai200::data pgvector postgres pgbouncer connection retake1

column1: Under PgBouncer transaction pooling, a session-level SET command stops working between transactions. What's the fix for a per-query setting like hnsw.ef_search?
column2: Use SET LOCAL hnsw.ef_search = 150; inside the transaction - it resets automatically at COMMIT/ROLLBACK, so it is safe with pooled connections; a plain session-level SET is lost once the connection returns to the pool.
column3: ai200::data pgvector postgres pgbouncer connection retake1

column1: What are PgBouncer's official default values on Azure for pool_mode, default_pool_size, and max_client_conn?
column2: pgbouncer.pool_mode = transaction, pgbouncer.default_pool_size = 50 (server connections per user/database pair), pgbouncer.max_client_conn = 5000 (max client-side connections); pgbouncer.query_wait_timeout defaults to 120 seconds.
column3: ai200::data pgvector postgres pgbouncer connection retake1

column1: Exam scenario: 200 Azure Functions instances each open their own direct Postgres connection per invocation and start hitting connection-limit errors under load. Two fixes?
column2: Enable built-in PgBouncer (General Purpose/Memory Optimized tier) and connect on 6432 with transaction pooling, plus a bounded client-side pool (psycopg_pool.ConnectionPool with a small max_size) instead of one raw connection per invocation.
column3: ai200::data pgvector postgres pgbouncer connection scenario retake1

column1: Exact max_connections ceiling by compute tier on Azure Database for PostgreSQL - name two.
column2: Burstable B1ms: 50 connections. General Purpose 4 vCores: 1,718. Memory Optimized 16 vCores: 5,000 - exceeding the tier's limit fails new connections, which is why pooling matters at scale.
column3: ai200::data pgvector postgres connection limits retake1

column1: Microsoft Entra authentication flow for psycopg against Azure Database for PostgreSQL - what do you request, and what goes in the password field?
column2: Call DefaultAzureCredential().get_token('https://ossrdbms-aad.database.windows.net/.default') and pass token.token as the connection password; the username must be in user@servername form - the token replaces a stored static password entirely.
column3: ai200::data pgvector postgres connect entra retake1

column1: Python pattern: how does pgvector.psycopg let you skip manual vector-literal casting when sending embeddings with psycopg 3?
column2: Call register_vector(conn) from pgvector.psycopg right after connecting; it registers adapters for a NumPy array and for pgvector's own Vector wrapper class (not a bare Python list), so either binds straight into a vector column or query parameter without building a string literal; wrap a plain list first, e.g. Vector([1,2,3]).
column3: ai200::data pgvector postgres sdk python retake1

column1: A vector(n) column can store more than 2,000 dimensions - can every pgvector index type use it?
column2: No. hnsw and ivfflat both cap out at 2,000 indexable dimensions (error: cannot have more than 2000 dimensions for index). For bigger embeddings (e.g. 3,072-dim text-embedding-3-large), use DiskANN (pg_diskann) instead - it indexes up to 16,000 dimensions once product_quantized = true (pg_diskann v0.6+).
column3: ai200::data postgres pgvector diskann indexing limits retake1

column1: What is DiskANN (pg_diskann) on Azure Database for PostgreSQL, and is it part of community pgvector?
column2: An Azure-specific extension (not upstream pgvector or community Postgres) implementing the DiskANN graph algorithm; like HNSW it needs no training step and can be built on an empty table, and it targets very large datasets (100M+ vectors) with high recall and low latency.

column1: DiskANN has build-time and query-time knobs, same idea as IVFFlat's lists/probes - name them and their defaults, plus how to force the planner to use the index.
column2: Build-time: max_neighbors (default 32, graph edges per node) and l_value_ib (build search-list size — Microsoft's own docs disagree on the default: the pgvector performance-tuning page says 50, the pg_diskann how-to page says 100 and recommends 100 at every dataset-size tier; run SHOW or check pg_indexes rather than trusting either figure blindly). Query-time: SET diskann.l_value_is = 100; (default 100, higher = more recall/slower). To force the index when the planner picks a seq scan: SET LOCAL enable_seqscan TO OFF;.
column3: ai200::data pgvector postgres diskann indexing retake1

column1: DiskANN's diskann.iterative_search setting - name its three modes and the default.
column2: relaxed_order (default): iteratively searches more of the graph in batches of l_value_is until LIMIT rows are found, possibly out of exact distance order. strict_order: same, but guarantees distance-sorted output. off: non-iterative - caps results at l_value_is regardless of LIMIT.
column3: ai200::data pgvector postgres diskann rag retake1

column1: Decision table - exact scan vs IVFFlat vs HNSW vs DiskANN: which needs existing data to train, which tolerates an empty table, and which scales best?
column2: Exact scan (no index): 100% recall, fine under ~10k rows. IVFFlat: k-means needs data loaded first, fastest/lightest build. HNSW: graph-based, works on an empty table, best recall/latency for most sizes. DiskANN (Azure-only): also empty-table-ready, built for 100M+ row scale with high recall; Microsoft's own pages disagree on build speed (a training module says 'fast build times', the how-to page says it takes more time than IVFFlat).
column3: ai200::data postgres pgvector indexing decisiontable retake1

column1: Exam scenario: a nightly job truncates a staging table, bulk-loads 2 million fresh embeddings with COPY, then swaps it into production. A teammate wants to pre-create the ANN index on the empty staging table before the COPY so indexing is already done when data lands. For IVFFlat specifically, why is this wrong?
column2: IVFFlat's lists are k-means clusters computed once, at build time, from whatever rows exist then - indexing an empty table produces meaningless, unusable centroids. Build IVFFlat after the COPY; if the index truly must exist before data lands, use HNSW instead, since its graph updates incrementally and tolerates starting from zero rows.
column3: ai200::data postgres pgvector indexing scenario mock01 retake1

column1: Exam scenario: two engineers argue over an IVFFlat index - one wants to raise lists from 1000 to 4000, the other wants to raise probes from 10 to 40. Which change needs a rebuild, which takes effect immediately, and which one improves recall for queries running right now?
column2: lists is a build-time structural choice - changing it means dropping and recreating the index. probes is a query-time/session setting (SET ivfflat.probes = 40;) that applies immediately, including to queries against the existing index right now - raising probes (not lists) is what improves recall today, at the cost of latency.
column3: ai200::data postgres pgvector indexing scenario mock01 retake1

column1: Official Azure sizing formulas for IVFFlat lists and probes, by table size?
column2: lists: rows / 1000 for up to 1M rows, sqrt(rows) above 1M (per the pgvector performance-tuning doc) - e.g. 4M rows gives roughly 2000 lists, so start probes around 45 (sqrt(2000)). probes: lists / 10 for up to 1M rows, sqrt(lists) above 1M. Conflicting official guidance: the Azure training module instead buckets large tables as 1M-10M rows → flat 4,000-10,000 lists and only switches to sqrt(rows) above 10M rows - so the SAME 4M-row table could reasonably target ~2000 (doc formula above) or ~4000-10000 (training module); verify which source the question wants before answering.

column1: HNSW build parameters m and ef_construction - defaults, and the rule of thumb for a high-quality index?
column2: Defaults: m = 16 (max connections per graph node), ef_construction = 64 (build-time candidate-list size). Rule of thumb: set ef_construction to at least 2x m, and 4x m for high-quality indexes - e.g. raising m to 32 for 99%+ recall suggests ef_construction around 128.

column1: How do you rebuild a degraded vector index on a live table without blocking writes, and how do you tell whether an existing index is even being used?
column2: Zero-downtime rebuild: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY under a temporary name (or REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY), verify with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, then swap in; track build progress via pg_stat_progress_create_index. To check usage, query pg_stat_user_indexes - idx_scan = 0 usually means the query's distance operator does not match the index's operator class, so Postgres silently falls back to a Seq Scan.
column3: ai200::data postgres pgvector indexing maintenance retake1

column1: Storage math for a vector column: formula, and the number for 1 million rows of 1536-dim float embeddings?
column2: dimensions x 4 bytes x row_count for the raw column (float4 per element) - a 1536-dim column costs about 6 KB/row, so about 6 GB for 1 million rows, before the index on top: per the Learn training module, HNSW index overhead is about 1.5-2x the vector column size and IVFFlat about 1-1.5x.

column1: JSONB metadata column vs separate structured columns for filtering a vector search - when does each win, and what index does JSONB need?
column2: Structured columns (INTEGER/NUMERIC/TIMESTAMPTZ) win when you filter or sort on known attributes - they get efficient B-tree indexes and accurate planner stats. JSONB wins for dynamic/sparse attributes, but only a GIN index speeds it up, and only for containment ops (@>, ?, ?|, ?&) - never for a numeric range filter, which instead needs an expression index on the cast value.
column3: ai200::data pgvector postgres jsonb indexing retake1

column1: Exam scenario: a RAG query filters WHERE category = 'legal' then does ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 10 using an HNSW index. For a rarely-used category, fewer than 10 rows come back even though more exist. Why, and what are two fixes?
column2: The ANN index returns its nearest neighbours first, then the filter discards most of them - for a small/rare category that undershoots LIMIT. Fixes: raise ef_search/probes to widen the pre-filter candidate pool, build a partial index scoped to that filter value, or (on DiskANN) switch diskann.iterative_search so it keeps expanding the search until LIMIT is satisfied.
column3: ai200::data postgres pgvector rag indexing scenario retake1

column1: What is a partial vector index, when is it worth building, and what's the trap with the query's WHERE clause?
column2: An index built on a subset of rows, e.g. CREATE INDEX ON docs USING ivfflat(embedding vector_cosine_ops) WITH (lists=100) WHERE tier = 'premium'; - smaller and faster for that slice. Trap: PostgreSQL only uses it when the query's WHERE clause matches the index definition's predicate exactly - a LIKE-based rewrite of an equality predicate will not match it.

column1: RAG pattern: why add a distance-threshold WHERE clause alongside LIMIT instead of just taking the top-k by distance?
column2: Plain LIMIT k always returns k rows even when nothing is actually relevant, which a downstream LLM then treats as ground truth. Add WHERE embedding <=> $1 < 0.4 (typical cosine thresholds run about 0.3 strict/high-precision to about 0.6 lenient/high-recall for OpenAI-style embeddings) so an empty result is possible and honest.

column1: Compute-tier vCore:memory ratios for vector workloads, and which scaling action actually restarts the server?
column2: Burstable 1-20 vCores at 2 GB/vCore, General Purpose 2-96 at 4 GB/vCore, Memory Optimized 2-96 at 8 GB/vCore (recommended so a large HNSW graph stays cached - aim for memory at least 1.5x the index size). Changing the compute tier/vCores always restarts the server; increasing storage size typically does not (and storage can only grow, never shrink).
column3: ai200::data pgvector postgres compute scaling retake1

column1: azure_ai extension: what schemas does it create, and what do you call to configure the Azure OpenAI endpoint and key before using it?
column2: Creates azure_ai (config), azure_openai, azure_cognitive, and azure_ml schemas. Configure with SELECT azure_ai.set_setting('azure_openai.endpoint', '...'); and SELECT azure_ai.set_setting('azure_openai.subscription_key', '...');, then generate embeddings in SQL with azure_openai.create_embeddings('<deployment>', input_text)::vector.
column3: ai200::data pgvector postgres azureai rag retake1

column1: # ---------- retake batch: redis (retake1) ----------
Azure Managed Redis: what are the four tiers and their memory-to-vCPU ratios?
column2: Memory Optimized 8:1 (dev/test, memory-heavy/low-throughput); Balanced 4:1 (general caching/session store); Compute Optimized 2:1 (max-throughput, smallest max size); Flash Optimized — RAM+NVMe, for very large (100s GB–TB) datasets with a hot/cold access split.

column1: Exam scenario: a team picks the cheapest tier, Flash Optimized, to store a multi-TB RediSearch vector index — will it work?
column2: No — Flash Optimized does not support RediSearch (so no vector search), RedisBloom, RedisTimeSeries, active geo-replication, or the Non-clustered policy; only RedisJSON runs there. Vector workloads need Memory Optimized, Balanced, or Compute Optimized.
column3: ai200::data redis tiers vector scenario retake1

column1: What is the default maxmemory eviction policy, and does it differ between OSS Redis and Azure Managed Redis?
column2: Yes: open-source Redis defaults to noeviction; Azure Managed Redis defaults to volatile-lru (only keys carrying a TTL are evicted) — always confirm the policy explicitly rather than assuming either default.

column1: Which clustering policy and eviction policy does enabling the RediSearch module force on an Azure Managed Redis instance?
column2: Enterprise clustering policy and the NoEviction eviction policy are both mandatory the moment RediSearch is enabled — plan extra memory headroom, since a full cache then returns write errors instead of evicting index entries.
column3: ai200::data redis vector eviction clustering retake1

column1: OSS vs Enterprise vs Non-clustered policy — what changes for the client?
column2: OSS: client connects straight to shards via the Redis Cluster API (needs a cluster-aware library; RediSearch unsupported). Enterprise: single endpoint, an internal proxy routes to shards (any standard client; RediSearch requires this). Non-clustered: single unsharded process, limited to caches ≤25 GB.

column1: redis-py: which client class connects to an OSS-clustering-policy Azure Managed Redis instance?
column2: redis.cluster.RedisCluster.from_url(url) — it discovers shards and follows redirections. An Enterprise or Non-clustered cache just uses the plain redis.Redis.from_url(url) client instead.

column1: Default Redis connection port: Azure Managed Redis vs. the older Azure Cache for Redis?
column2: Azure Managed Redis (Redis Enterprise-based) uses port 10000; the older Azure Cache for Redis (Basic/Standard/Premium, community-edition Redis) uses port 6380 — mixing the two up is a classic "can't connect" cause.

column1: Exam scenario: default auth for a brand-new Azure Managed Redis cache, and the CLI command to verify the connection?
column2: Default is Microsoft Entra ID (password-free; managed identity is enabled automatically) — access keys still work but are the legacy fallback, and Entra auth is SSL-only. Verify with az redisenterprise test-connection --name <cache> --resource-group <rg> --auth entra.

column1: Azure Managed Redis modules — what is each one actually for?
column2: RediSearch: search engine + secondary index + vector KNN. RedisBloom: probabilistic structures (Bloom/Cuckoo filter, count-min sketch, top-k) — trade perfect accuracy for speed/memory. RedisTimeSeries: high-throughput time-series (IoT/monitoring). RedisJSON: store and query nested JSON documents.

column1: Can you add a Redis module, or change the clustering policy, on an Azure Managed Redis cache after it is created?
column2: No — modules and clustering policy are both fixed at creation time; adding a module or switching policy later means provisioning a new instance and migrating data (the one exception: a Non-clustered cache can later move to a clustered policy).

column1: Exam scenario: choose FLAT or HNSW for a RediSearch vector index?
column2: FLAT (brute-force/exact) for small datasets — roughly under 10,000 vectors — or when perfect accuracy matters. HNSW (graph-based, approximate) for larger datasets needing sub-10 ms KNN with 95–99% recall — the default choice for production AI systems.

column1: A RediSearch vector query errors out vs. silently returns garbage — which misconfiguration causes which?
column2: A DIM mismatch (query-vector length ≠ the index's DIM) makes Redis reject the data or query outright. A wrong DISTANCE_METRIC (e.g. L2 on COSINE-trained text embeddings) causes no error at all — it just silently returns semantically irrelevant matches.

column1: RediSearch DISTANCE_METRIC choices — when do you use COSINE vs L2 vs IP?
column2: COSINE — text/semantic embeddings (angle only; the OpenAI/Cohere/sentence-transformer default). L2 (Euclidean) — image/spatial embeddings (magnitude and direction both matter). IP (inner product) — only for already-normalized embeddings.

column1: Store vector embeddings in a Redis HASH or in RedisJSON — how do you decide?
column2: HASH: flat fields only, vector stored as raw bytes, smallest memory and fastest queries — the default choice for simple metadata. JSON: supports nested objects and multiple vectors per document at some memory/latency cost — pick it when the data model needs structure.

column1: RediSearch: syntax for a metadata-filtered ("hybrid") KNN search, and for a distance threshold instead of top-K?
column2: Hybrid: put the filter before the arrow — @category:{docs}=>[KNN 5 @embedding $vec] filters first, then finds the K nearest inside that subset. Threshold instead of fixed K: @embedding:[VECTOR_RANGE 0.2 $vec]=>{$YIELD_DISTANCE_AS: score} returns every vector inside that distance.

column1: Is "semantic caching" a managed Azure Redis feature you just turn on?
column2: No — it is an application or API-gateway pattern built on top of RediSearch vector search, not a distinct managed feature. Build it with RedisVL's SemanticCache (app-level) or Azure API Management's llm-semantic-cache-lookup/llm-semantic-cache-store policies (gateway-level).

column1: RedisVL SemanticCache's distance_threshold — what are the units, and which direction is "stricter"?
column2: It is a COSINE distance in the range 0 to 2 — lower means stricter (near-identical prompts only); raising the threshold returns more cache hits at the risk of reusing a semantically-wrong answer.

column1: Redis pub/sub vs Streams — what is the delivery guarantee for each?
column2: Pub/sub: PUBLISH/SUBSCRIBE, at-most-once, fire-and-forget, no persistence — a message published while nobody is subscribed is gone forever. Streams: XADD/XREADGROUP/XACK with consumer groups, durable and retryable — unacknowledged tasks sit in a pending list for reclaim.

column1: Exam scenario: three worker instances all subscribe to the same pub/sub channel to split an inference workload — what actually happens?
column2: All three workers receive and process every message — pub/sub broadcasts, it never load-balances — tripling compute and producing duplicate results. Use a Streams consumer group instead so each message is delivered to exactly one consumer.

column1: Why can "Used Memory" look like double your dataset size, and what should you alert on instead?
column2: With High Availability enabled, Used Memory counts both primary and replica shards, so ~10 GB of data can report as ~20 GB — expected, not a leak. Alert on Used Memory Percentage instead (already normalized to the SKU limit); plan to scale before it is consistently above 75%.

column1: Why does Microsoft's own guidance say never run KEYS in production Redis?
column2: Each Redis shard is single-threaded — KEYS is an O(n) command that blocks every other command until it finishes scanning the whole keyspace. Use SCAN instead: it walks the keyspace in small cursor-based increments without blocking.

column1: Exam scenario: pick the right cache-invalidation strategy — simple time-bound staleness, an update that must be visible immediately, or notifying other app instances?
column2: Time-bound staleness is acceptable → TTL expiry. Must be correct right after a write → delete-on-write (cache-aside: update DB, then delete the key). Several app instances each hold their own copy that must all clear together → pub/sub-driven invalidation broadcast.

column1: Exam scenario: choose an eviction policy for (a) a pure ephemeral cache, (b) a keyspace mixing permanent app-state keys with TTL'd cache keys, and (c) a RediSearch-enabled instance?
column2: (a) Every key disposable → allkeys-lru/allkeys-lfu. (b) Some keys must never disappear → volatile-lru/volatile-lfu/volatile-ttl, which only ever evict keys that have a TTL, leaving no-TTL keys untouched. (c) RediSearch enabled → noeviction is mandatory, so size for headroom instead of relying on eviction.

column1: Exam scenario: what do TTL/PTTL return, and what do PERSIST and a plain re-SET do to an existing TTL?
column2: TTL/PTTL return -1 = key exists with no expiry, -2 = key does not exist. PERSIST key removes the TTL (a later TTL call then returns -1). A plain SET key value with no KEEPTTL option also silently discards any existing TTL — add KEEPTTL to preserve it.

column1: Exam scenario: a Function's managed identity must only read secret VALUES from Key Vault — never list, create, or delete them. Which role fits, and what are the two traps?
column2: Key Vault Secrets User — read secret contents only. Trap 1: Key Vault Secrets Officer also creates/updates/deletes secrets, too broad for a read-only consumer. Trap 2: Key Vault Reader reads only metadata, never the secret value.

column1: Key Vault Crypto User vs Key Vault Crypto Officer — what is the difference?
column2: Key Vault Crypto User performs cryptographic operations (encrypt, decrypt, sign, verify, wrap, unwrap) with existing keys. Key Vault Crypto Officer can do that and manage the keys themselves (create, import, delete, rotate) — everything except managing role assignments.

column1: Key Vault Certificate User vs Key Vault Certificates Officer — which is for an app that just loads a TLS certificate, and which manages the certificate lifecycle?
column2: Key Vault Certificate User — narrow role, reads the entire certificate including its private key, built for apps binding TLS. Key Vault Certificates Officer — broader lifecycle role: create, import, delete certificates and manage issuers/policies.

column1: Which Key Vault role can purge a soft-deleted vault, and which role only manages role assignments for the other Key Vault data-plane roles?
column2: Key Vault Purge Operator permanently deletes (purges) soft-deleted vaults/objects. Key Vault Data Access Administrator is a separate meta-role that adds/removes role assignments for the other Key Vault data roles — neither one can itself read a secret value.

column1: Exam scenario: a user holds Key Vault Contributor on a vault that still uses the legacy access-policy model. Why is that risky?
column2: Key Vault Contributor is control-plane only and can't read data directly, but on an access-policy vault it can set its own access policy and self-grant data access — tightly restrict who holds Contributor, even though its name sounds like a data role.

column1: As of which Key Vault API version did Azure RBAC become the DEFAULT permission model for newly created vaults, replacing legacy access policies as the default?
column2: API version 2026-02-01 and later — new vaults default to Azure RBAC; existing vaults keep whatever model they were created with unless you explicitly switch them.

column1: Exam scenario: you recover a soft-deleted Key Vault. Do its old RBAC role assignments and Event Grid subscriptions come back automatically?
column2: No — both are deleted when the vault is soft-deleted and are not restored on recovery; you must recreate every role assignment and event subscription by hand afterward.

column1: Key Vault throttling: GET limit per vault per 10 seconds, write limit, and the subscription-wide ceiling?
column2: 4,000 secret GETs per vault per 10-second window per region; writes (create/import) share 300 per 10 seconds; a subscription's total across all its vaults in a region caps at 5× one vault's limit — past that, Key Vault returns HTTP 429 and expects exponential backoff.

column1: DefaultAzureCredential — what does it try first on a deployed Azure service vs on a developer's laptop?
column2: It chains credentials in order (environment variables → workload identity → managed identity → Azure CLI → Azure Developer CLI → PowerShell), stopping at the first that works — a deployed app gets managed identity automatically while a developer's az login session is used locally, with no code change.

column1: App Configuration built-in roles — which two are data-plane, and which two are control-plane only?
column2: Data plane: App Configuration Data Owner (read/write/delete key-values) and App Configuration Data Reader (read-only). Control plane: App Configuration Contributor and App Configuration Reader manage/read the resource itself — though Contributor can also enable access-key auth and then read/write data that way.

column1: Exam scenario: an app reads config through the App Configuration provider, and one value is a Key Vault reference. Which TWO role assignments does the app's identity need, and on what resources?
column2: App Configuration Data Reader on the App Configuration store (to read the reference pointer) and Key Vault Secrets User on the Key Vault (to resolve the actual secret) — App Configuration never stores the secret value itself, only the vault URI/name, so both assignments are required independently.

column1: Python azure-appconfiguration-provider: what are the default values of refresh_interval and secret_refresh_interval, and what happens if you never set secret_refresh_interval?
column2: refresh_interval defaults to 30 seconds (minimum 1s) and gates how often a config.refresh() call actually checks the sentinel key. secret_refresh_interval has no default — if you never set it, resolved Key Vault secrets are not periodically re-resolved; they only refresh when a full config refresh fires.

column1: Which App Configuration provider languages can monitor ALL selected keys for changes (not just one sentinel key) — does the Python provider?
column2: The .NET, JavaScript, Go, Spring, and Kubernetes providers can watch an entire key set; the Python provider cannot — in Python, refresh_on with a WatchKey sentinel is the only supported refresh trigger.

column1: Can a single App Configuration SettingSelector combine snapshot_name with a key_filter or label_filter?
column2: No — snapshot_name is mutually exclusive with key_filter, label_filter, and tag_filters on a SettingSelector; loading a snapshot means loading everything frozen in that point-in-time snapshot, nothing else.

column1: In an Azure built-in role's JSON definition, how do you tell at a glance whether a permission is control-plane or data-plane?
column2: Permissions under Actions are control-plane (authorized via Azure Resource Manager); permissions under DataActions are data-plane (authorized against the service's own data endpoint) — a role can have both, but a pure management role like App Configuration Contributor has Actions only.

column1: Exam scenario: a Function only publishes messages and never receives them — once on Service Bus and once on Event Hubs. Least-privilege role for each?
column2: Azure Service Bus Data Sender (Service Bus) and Azure Event Hubs Data Sender (Event Hubs) — both services share the same Data Owner / Data Sender / Data Receiver pattern, so send-only always maps to the Sender role, never Owner or Receiver.
column3: ai200::ops servicebus eventhubs roles scenario retake1

column1: Event Grid: which role actually lets an identity SEND/publish events to a topic, versus the roles that only manage event subscriptions or topics?
column2: EventGrid Data Sender — data-plane, publishes events. EventGrid EventSubscription Contributor/Reader are control-plane: they manage or read event subscriptions (routing config), not event data; EventGrid Contributor manages the topic/domain resources themselves, also control-plane.

column1: Exam scenario: a Function app's managed identity needs AzureWebJobsStorage access. Storage Blob Data Contributor seems enough — what does the host actually require, and why?
column2: Storage Blob Data Owner — the Functions host needs blob-lease permissions (for singleton locks, e.g. the Timer trigger) that plain Storage Blob Data Contributor doesn't fully cover; add Storage Table Data Contributor too if you want host diagnostic events logged.

column1: Storage Queue data-plane roles — which one only adds messages, and which one only peeks/retrieves/deletes them?
column2: Storage Queue Data Message Sender — add messages only. Storage Queue Data Message Processor — peek, retrieve, and delete messages (consumer side). Storage Queue Data Contributor is the broad role covering both plus queue management.

column1: Exam scenario: az role assignment create --role "Cosmos DB Built-in Data Reader" fails to find that role. Why, and what command actually works?
column2: Cosmos DB for NoSQL's data-plane roles (Cosmos DB Built-in Data Reader, Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor) are native to the account, not standard Azure RBAC — assign them with az cosmosdb sql role assignment create instead; the Azure portal doesn't support managing them at all.

column1: ACR access roles: how do the classic AcrPull/AcrPush differ from the newer Container Registry Repository Reader/Writer/Contributor roles?
column2: AcrPull/AcrPush/AcrDelete are registry-wide and defined via Actions (not DataActions) even though they govern image data. The newer Container Registry Repository Reader/Writer/Contributor roles use true DataActions and can scope to a single repository — finer-grained least privilege.

column1: AKS: Azure Kubernetes Service RBAC Reader vs RBAC Writer — why does Reader deliberately exclude Secrets?
column2: RBAC Reader can view most namespace objects but explicitly can't read Secrets — reading a Secret exposes a ServiceAccount's credentials, letting a reader impersonate that ServiceAccount (privilege escalation). RBAC Writer can read Secrets, so grant it only when that risk is acceptable.

column1: Does Azure Managed Redis use Azure RBAC data-plane roles like Storage's, to control who can run commands against the cache?
column2: No — Microsoft Entra principals are added directly as cache users via the portal's Authentication blade and get full access to all commands/keys by default; there is no Redis Data Reader/Contributor role, only a preview custom data-access-permission feature for finer control.

column1: Exam scenario: an app's managed identity must push custom metrics to Azure Monitor and do nothing else. Which role, and how does it differ from Monitoring Reader?
column2: Monitoring Metrics Publisher — data-plane, write-only (Microsoft.Insights/Metrics/Write). Monitoring Reader is the opposite: a broad read role that can read all metrics/logs and even run Log Analytics queries, but can't publish anything.

Exam scenario: two services in a RAG pipeline export telemetry to the same Application Insights resource, but the Application Map shows one unnamed node instead of two. Fix?
column2: Set a distinct service.name OpenTelemetry resource attribute per service (optionally add service.namespace). Application Insights derives the cloud role name from service.namespace.service.name (falls back to service.name alone); leave both unset and every service defaults to the Application Insights resource's own name, which is why they collapse into one map node.

column1: Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry Python Distro: if both code and an environment variable configure the same setting, who wins — for the connection string, and for sampling?
column2: Opposite rules: for configure_azure_monitor(connection_string=...) vs APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING, code wins. For sampling_ratio= vs OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER/OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG, the environment variable wins. A classic trap when code and deployment env vars disagree.

column1: Of the 5 OpenTelemetry span kinds, which 2 does Application Insights route to the requests table instead of dependencies?
column2: SpanKind.SERVER (inbound HTTP) and SpanKind.CONSUMER (processing a pulled queue message) — both count as work the service received. CLIENT, INTERNAL, and PRODUCER (the default when no kind is set) all land in dependencies.

column1: In the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry Distro for Python, what sampler applies if you call configure_azure_monitor() and configure zero sampling settings?
column2: Not "always on" — the Distro defaults to a RateLimitedSampler capping traces per second, not a fixed percentage and not always_on. A reasonable manual starting ratio if you do set one is around 0.05 (5%).

column1: Which Python libraries/frameworks does the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry Distro auto-instrument with zero manual span code?
column2: requests, urllib/urllib3, inbound Flask/Django/FastAPI, psycopg2, Azure SDK client calls, and Python's standard logging module — anything else (e.g. a custom embedding call) needs a manual span.

column1: Exam scenario: inside with tracer.start_as_current_span(...) as span: your code catches an exception, logs it, and does NOT re-raise. Does the span show an error status in Application Insights?
column2: No — the SDK only auto-records the exception and sets an error status for exceptions that propagate out of the span block. A caught-and-handled exception needs an explicit span.record_exception(ex) plus span.set_status(Status(StatusCode.ERROR, "...")).

column1: The Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry exporter loses connectivity to the ingestion endpoint. What's the built-in resilience behavior?
column2: It caches telemetry to a local temp-directory subfolder and retries for up to 48 hours. Override the path with storage_directory=, or (not recommended for production) disable it entirely with disable_offline_storage=True.

column1: Classic Application Insights table/column names vs workspace-based Log Analytics equivalents — where does the naive "just add App + PascalCase" renaming pattern actually break?
column2: Most follow it (requests → AppRequests, dependencies → AppDependencies, exceptions → AppExceptions, traces → AppTraces), but customEvents → AppEvents and customMetrics → AppMetrics break it. Columns rename too: operation_Id → OperationId, cloud_RoleName → AppRoleName, timestamp → TimeGenerated.

column1: KQL: dcount() vs count_distinct() — when would you deliberately pick the slower one?
column2: dcount() is an approximate, cheap, probabilistic estimate — the default choice at scale. count_distinct() is exact but far more resource-intensive, so reserve it for small result sets where an exact distinct count genuinely matters.

column1: You write Table1 | join (Table2) on Key with no kind= specified. What join actually runs?
column2: kind=innerunique (the default) — an inner join that first deduplicates the left table per join key, which can silently drop legitimate duplicate left rows. Use kind=inner explicitly when every matching row combination must be preserved.

column1: Exam scenario: Application Insights sampling is active, and exceptions | summarize count() by type reports far fewer errors than you know occurred. Fix the query.
column2: Use summarize sum(itemCount) by type instead. Each sampled row's itemCount states how many real events it represents; plain count() only counts surviving sampled rows and silently undercounts true volume.

column1: Exam scenario: during an incident you must interactively filter telemetry by service, time window, and error type to find a root cause. Dashboard, Workbook, or Alert rule?
column2: Workbook — parameterized, drill-down steps built for ad-hoc investigation. Dashboards are static tiles on a scheduled refresh for at-a-glance ongoing monitoring (not real-time); alert rules only evaluate a condition and notify, they don't let you explore.

column1: Observability vocabulary ladder: metrics vs logs vs traces, and span vs trace vs operation_Id — how do the two ladders line up?
column2: Metrics = cheap aggregated numeric time series; logs = rich structured records (traces/exceptions tables, KQL-queried); traces (distributed tracing) = the causally-linked span tree for one request. Inside a trace: a span is one operation, a trace is the whole OpenTelemetry tree sharing one trace ID, and operation_Id is the Application Insights column holding that same ID, joining requests/dependencies/traces/exceptions rows for one request.

column1: Exam scenario: a Container Apps revision is crash-looping and you need the container's stdout/stderr from Log Analytics. Which table — and what's the AKS equivalent?
column2: Container Apps console logs live in ContainerAppConsoleLogs_CL (platform events in ContainerAppSystemLogs_CL). On AKS the equivalent is ContainerLogV2 — the legacy ContainerLog table's support retired 2026-09-30 (already past as of this retake), so ContainerLogV2 is now the only current answer.
